lesson.title: Wie oft? immer, oft, manchmal, selten, einmal
lesson.subtitle: frequency without a helping verb — five single words doing English's -ly work

hook.title: English Needs a Helper, German Doesn't
hook.content: To say how often in English you reach for a helper: I always drink coffee, I often drink coffee, I sometimes drink coffee. German needs none of that — immer, oft, manchmal are single words that drop straight into the sentence and stay put. There is no do-support, no -ly, no position rule to memorise. Two of the five hide a shift you already own: selten is seldom's twin wearing Tag's badge — German hardened seldom's seld- to selt- while English kept the D — and einmal is ein + Mal — one + time — the same doubling that built zweimal in topic 5. English kept the -mal half of that family and lost the German word for it.

footnotes.title: The Mal Family
footnotes.content: Jedes Mal, ein Mal, zwei Mal — English and German split this word's jobs. English kept the root as the noun meal — das Mal's old twin, both from a root meaning 'mark, measure' — and built once and twice on it; German kept das Mal as noun AND built einmal, zweimal, dreimal on it. Both languages still say it: once and once.

pattern.title: Where the Frequency Word Lands
pattern.content: Default slot: right after the verb, before the object. Ich trinke immer Kaffee (I always drink coffee). Freestyle fronting for emphasis: Immer trinke ich Kaffee — the adverb takes position 1 and pushes the conjugated verb to position 2, the same swap you do with heute and morgen. With negation: Ich trinke nicht oft Kaffee; nie is the absolute ('never') and sits exactly where nicht would. And the one-off: einmal means 'once', and its opposite einmalig is not needed — Einmal im Jahr fahre ich ans Meer does the job with an ordinary time phrase.
pattern.linguist_note: German's frequency adverbs are uninflected single words, which is why they never drift away from the verb. English bolted them on with -ly and let them wander to the front of the sentence; German's wandered and settled back into the same slot every time.

exercises.prompt: Frequency — match each sentence with its reading:

matching_pairs.english: I always drink coffee in the morning
matching_pairs.german: Ich trinke immer Kaffee am Morgen

matching_pairs.english: Once a year I go to the sea
matching_pairs.german: Einmal im Jahr fahre ich ans Meer

exercises.target_answer: Ich trinke immer Kaffee am Morgen, Wir haben oft Zeit, Manchmal lese ich ein Buch, Ich trinke selten Kaffee, Einmal im Jahr fahre ich ans Meer
exercises.meaning: always, often, sometimes, seldom, once a year
exercises.explanation: No helper verb anywhere: always/never/often/sometimes/once are all single German words sitting after the conjugated verb.

exercises.prompt: 'Ich trinke _____ Kaffee.' (I seldom drink coffee) — which word wears the D→T badge?
exercises.meaning: selten ↔ seldom: German hardened the D to T (seld- → selt-), English kept the D
exercises.explanation: selten is seldom's twin, and Tag's law is at work in it: German hardened the d of seld- to t (selt-), while English kept the D. Same word, same meaning — the shift simply worked on the German side.

exercises.prompt: Fronted for emphasis: '_____ trinke ich Kaffee.' (Always I drink coffee):
exercises.meaning: Immer trinke ich Kaffee = always I drink coffee
exercises.explanation: Fronting a frequency adverb swaps positions 1 and 2: the adverb takes position 1, and the conjugated verb (trinke) moves up behind it. Same rule as heute and morgen.

exercises.prompt: 'einmal' = one + Mal — and das Mal has an English twin hiding in plain sight. What is the English word that survives?
exercises.meaning: das Mal ↔ meal: the same old 'mark, measure' root, each language keeping a piece
exercises.explanation: das Mal is meal's twin — both from an ancient root meaning 'mark, measure' (English still keeps it in piecemeal). German kept das Mal as noun AND built the adverbs (einmal, zweimal) on it; English built once and twice on the same root. Time is a different root entirely.

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'I always drink coffee in the morning'
exercises.target_answer: Ich trinke immer Kaffee am Morgen
exercises.meaning: I always drink coffee in the morning

vocab_hints.note: immer goes straight after the conjugated verb — no helping word, no -ly. Ich trinke immer Kaffee.

exercises.explanation: Verb in slot 2, immer in the slot behind it, then the object. am Morgen folds an + dem into one word — the dative of time; the accusative version is jeden Morgen, 'every morning'.

summary.outcome: Answer 'how often?' with one word, and slot it after the verb without a helper.
summary.takeaway: immer, oft, manchmal, selten, einmal — five helperless adverbs, and selten is English seldom's D→T twin.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: point-in-time adverbs — jetzt, sofort, später, früh, endlich.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from Wie oft? immer, oft, manchmal, selten, einmal (I always drink coffee in the morning):
twist.target_answer: Ich trinke immer Kaffee am Morgen
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Ich trinke immer Kaffee am Morgen" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of Wie oft? immer, oft, manchmal, selten, einmal without relying on short-term echo.

immer.context_phrase: Ich trinke immer Kaffee am Morgen.
immer.context_translation: I always drink coffee in the morning.
immer.etymology_derivation: OHG iomēr 'ever + more' — cognate with Middle English 'a mare' (evermore). [wiktionary]

oft.context_translation: We often play in the park.
oft.etymology_derivation: Old High German ofta — the true twin of English oft/often. [wiktionary]

manchmal.context_translation: Sometimes I go to the cinema.
manchmal.etymology_derivation: manch (many a) + Mal (time, the meal-word cousin) — 'many a time'. [wiktionary]

selten.etymology_derivation: West Germanic *seldanā — the twin of English seldom, which the page lists as a cognate; German hardened d into t (seld- to selt-). [wiktionary]

einmal.context_phrase: Einmal im Jahr fahre ich ans Meer.
einmal.context_translation: Once a year I go to the sea.
einmal.etymology_derivation: ein 'one' + Mal 'time': Middle High German einmāle — literally one-time, hence once. [wiktionary]

morgen.etymology_derivation: Cognate with English morrow (hence to-morrow) and morn — both descend from the Germanic root for "morning". [wiktionary]

heute.etymology_derivation: Literally 'on this day': heu- is the he- of here/him, and the old ending hid Tag (day). English's own twin hēodæġ died out — today won. [wiktionary]

zeit.etymology_derivation: t → z [ts] (cognate with English "tide", as in Yuletide or time and tide).

trinken.context_translation: I drink a glass of water.

schweinefleisch.etymology_derivation: Schweinefleisch — a compound of Schwein (pig) and Fleisch (flesh, meat); Wiktionary compares the exact English calque swineflesh, so swine and flesh are both true cognates here. [wiktionary]

möglich.etymology_derivation: From mögen 'to be able' + -lich: literally may-ly, what may happen — mögen goes back to the same PIE root *megʰ- that produced English may. [wiktionary] [etymonline]

wespe.context_phrase: Eine Wespe sitzt auf dem Kuchen.
wespe.context_translation: A wasp sits on the cake.
wespe.etymology_derivation: From Old High German wefsa, from Proto-West Germanic *wapsu, from Proto-Germanic *wapsō, related to the verb web. English wasp is the listed cognate. [wiktionary]

anfang.context_translation: At the beginning it was hard.
anfang.etymology_derivation: an + Fang, catch — from anfangen, to catch at and so to begin; the entry lists archaic English fang, to seize, as a cognate. [wiktionary]

haushalt.etymology_derivation: Haus + halten, and the page lists English household as a cognate — the exact mirror, with halten the twin of hold (d to t). [wiktionary]

tat.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *dādi; the page compares English deed — the same do-word with the d to t hardening, as in day and Tag. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
